newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura scandal spotlights Japan economy's dark side.
newsitem.headline: Nomura scandal spotlights Japan economy's dark side.

text.p: News that executives at Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Ltd did irregular deals with a client apparently linked to racketeers has again thrown a spotlight on the dark side of Japan's economy.
The latest revelations also point to the tough road ahead as Japan tries to boost its financial industry's global competitiveness through a five-year "Big Bang" reform plan.

Nomura Vice President Atsushi Saito said on Thursday that two Nomura directors had made apparently discretionary transactions and moved profits raised from Nomura's own funds to the customer's account.
He said such actions are illegal as they violate the Securities and Exchange Law and that the case was under investigation by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC).

Saito said that he could not at the moment confirm media reports that the corporate client was run by a relative of a "sokaiya" racketeer. But he added that the client had a longstanding relationship with the two directors and family ties to a Nomura shareholder.
Sokaiya, often linked to Japan's "yakuza" crime syndicates, typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices.
Companies have also been known to hire them to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions at annual meetings.

The news comes six years after the 1991 resignation of top executives at Nomura and Nikko Securities following revelations that the brokerages had compensated favoured clients for losses and that their affiliates had dealings with organised crime.
Ryutaro Hashimoto -- now Japan's prime minister -- resigned his post as finance minister in the same year as a gesture of atonement for his ministry's failure to prevent the scandals.
Hashimoto, who is now touting the "Big Bang" financial reforms as a key pillar of his economic platform, reacted angrily to the latest incident, Japanese media said.
"Why do such things keep happening?" he fumed to reporters.
Links to what one newspaper called "the dark continent" within Japan's economy are hardly the monopoly of brokerages.

Last June the president of prestigious department store Takashimaya resigned to take management responsibility for the arrests of a former executive and two company officials on suspicion of making payoffs to sokaiya.

Ties between financial firms and yakuza grabbed attention last year when the government budgeted taxpayers' money to help wind up failed mortgage firms -- a hefty chunk of whose bad loans officials themselves said involved organised crime money.

The alleged role of gangsters at Japan's harbours has also been whispered to be one factor foiling a resolution of a U.S.-Japan dispute over port practices that could lead to trade sanctions on Japanese shipping companies next month.

"Involvement with the underworld is not something that brokerages have a monopoly on," said one financial analyst. "In the banking industry, the real estate industry, at corporations in general, it is very much a part of doing business in Japan."

That said, the Nomura scandal comes at a touchy time for the financial sector, given plans for sweeping reforms that will boost the need for surveillance as well as require management to change many of its long-time business practices.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the Nomura incident would not put the brakes on the "Big Bang" reforms and analysts agreed it was unlikely to have a direct impact.
Some analysts took the SESC probe of Nomura as a sign that the watchdog was prepared to do its job and do it well.
"It's a shot in the arm for the SESC, which was decried as a watchdog which neither barks nor bites," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
The SESC -- set up in the wake of the 1991 brokerage scandals -- declined comment on the Nomura case including media reports that it was seeking legal action against the brokerage.
Others said the incident shows that the real challenge for financial executives who must cope with the openly competitive market which "Big Bang" aims at lies inside their own heads.

"There is a mind-set problem for all financial institutions. They have to put the shareholder, not the company, first," said Brian Waterhouse, financial analyst at HSBC James Capel. "You can change the laws as much as you like with the 'Big Bang' but unless you change the mind-set, you are not going to get a more efficient financial system."
